opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because "AI" covers a lot of different needs, and customers show up at very different points.

Roughly, I'd split it into a few buckets.

The first group is still at the very beginning. They know they want to do something with generative AI, maybe they've played with a chatbot internally, but they don't know which use cases are worth it or how to get from demo to production. With them it's less about any specific tool and more about helping them pick a problem where AI can be measured and actually move a business metric, and then building the first version quickly so they learn something.

The second group, and honestly it's the biggest one we see now, has built prototypes and is stuck on quality. The demo works 70 or 80 percent of the time, and they can't ship it because they don't trust it. The help they need is mostly about evaluation: how do you define what "good" means for your application, how do you build an eval set, how do you get domain experts to give feedback efficiently, and how do you systematically improve things, whether that's better retrieval, better prompts, tuning a model, or changing the system design. A lot of what we've been building is aimed at this, because we think that's the real bottleneck. It's not access to models. Everyone has access to great models now. It's knowing whether your system is good enough and how to make it better.

The third group is already in production and cares about operational concerns: cost, latency, governance, security, who can access what data, monitoring for drift or regressions when a model provider updates something. That's where having AI sit right next to your data platform really matters. The same permissions and lineage that apply to your tables should apply to your models, your agents, and the tools they call.

Cutting across all of these is a question of how much customization people want. Some just want to call a frontier model with good retrieval over their data. Others have very specialized tasks where a smaller, tuned model is cheaper and better. We try not to be dogmatic about it. Our general view is that most real applications end up being compound AI systems, with multiple components, models, retrievers, and tools, and the job is to help people build, evaluate, and govern that whole system rather than just pick a model.

So the short answer is that we listen for where they're stuck. Usually it's not "which model should I use." It's "how do I know this works, and how do I make it work reliably on my data."

r001.rationale: The response describes customers’ needs by development stage and mentions both practical guidance and platform capabilities, but it does not clearly distinguish customers seeking AI infrastructure from those seeking Databricks’ hands-on collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we talk to customers, I think there are really two or three fairly distinct buckets, and it helps to separate them because the needs are pretty different.

The first bucket is companies that want to build something on top of existing models. They're not training a foundation model from scratch; they've got an enterprise use case, they have a lot of their own data, and they want to connect a model to that data and get it to do something useful and reliable. That's honestly the majority of what we see. And what they actually need there isn't a bigger model, it's the whole surrounding system: retrieval over their documents, tool calling against their internal APIs, governance over who can access what, evaluation so they know whether the thing is actually working, and monitoring once it's in production. We ended up calling this "compound AI systems" because the model is one component, but most of the engineering is in everything around it.

The second bucket is companies that want to customize or train models. That's a smaller set, but it's growing, and it's a lot of the reason we did the MosaicML acquisition. Sometimes it's fine-tuning an open model on their data; sometimes it's pretraining a domain-specific model because the general ones just don't know their vocabulary, like in biology or finance or legal. For them the ask is really about infrastructure: making training efficient and reliable at scale, dealing with hardware failures, getting the cost down so it's actually economical to iterate.

And then there's a third thing, which cuts across both, which is just the data side. People underestimate how much of AI development is data engineering. Cleaning, deduplicating, labeling, building evaluation sets, tracking lineage. A lot of customers come to us thinking they have an AI problem and it turns out they have a data problem first. That's actually where Databricks started, so it's a natural fit.

So when someone comes in, the first question we ask is basically: are you trying to build an application, or are you trying to build a model? And then what's the state of your data? The answers to those pretty much determine what help they actually need.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes application building, model training, and data work, and mentions infrastructure needs. It does not distinguish customers seeking infrastructure from those seeking Databricks’ hands-on collaboration in AI development.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two broad categories. One is customers who want to build AI applications. They have some business problem, and they want help figuring out how to use their data, which models to use, and how to evaluate whether the application is actually working. They don’t necessarily want to train a model; they want a system that solves the problem reliably.

Then there are customers who want to develop or customize the models themselves. They might need capabilities that an off-the-shelf model doesn’t provide, or they care about controlling the cost and performance for a particular workload. They need more of the infrastructure for training, fine-tuning, and serving models.

Those overlap, but the starting point is different: are you trying to build an application, or is developing the model itself a core part of what you do?

r001.rationale: It contrasts customers who want help shaping AI applications—including data, model choice, and evaluation—with customers who need infrastructure to train, fine-tune, and serve models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two broad categories. One is customers who want to use AI to help them develop things: write code, build data pipelines, analyze their data. The other is customers who want to build AI into their own applications and products.

For that second group, the challenge is usually less about getting a model to answer a question and more about getting it to work reliably with their data. How do you connect it to the right information, evaluate whether the answers are good, and improve it over time? They want help with that whole development process, not just access to a model.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes customers using AI to develop things from customers embedding AI in their products. It does not clearly distinguish customers seeking AI infrastructure from those seeking Databricks’ hands-on collaboration in AI development.
